Header: Candidatus Liberibacter africanus, L. americanus and L. asiaticus

Prevention: This disease is transmitted by the psyllid vector
Remove alternative hosts (eg. wild plants, other citrus spp) from around the field
Encourage natural enemy populations in the orchard (e.g., spiders, lacewings, predatory mites, ladybird beetles, hover flies) by reducing pesticide use in the general area
Citrus greening symptoms can be confused with zinc deficiency.
So use appropriate fertilizers containing zinc micronutrient to avoid confusion
Enforce phytosanitary measures: it is difficult to ensure plants are free from eggs and nymphs so importation of planting material from affected areas should be prohibited
Only clean and healthy plants, without any insects on them, should be transported & transplanted into new plantations
Monitoring: Monitor regularly the whole year for presence of psyllids and disease symptoms to avoid it spreading
Adults feeding on leaves resemble winged aphids 2)
Orange/yellow eggs appearing on the edges of tender young leaves 3)
Raised bumps on the underside of leaves hide nymphs, which are small green/ yellow scale-like insects
Leaves: pale- yellow, yellow veins and blotchy mottling 2)
Whole tree: sparsely foliated, extensive branch dieback and reduced size 3)
Fruits: small, lopsided and poorly colored with aborted seeds, severe fruit drop
Act quickly as soon as symptoms of the disease are seen or when the vector is detected
Direct Control: If only a few branches are affected, prune them immediately and bury them more than 60cm deep
It is important to destroy only very severely infected trees not producing economical yield
Disinfect tools after pruning each tree with bleach
Remove any young citrus trees that become infected, as they will never produce fruits and replace with disease free planting material
Restrictions: There are no registered insecticides in
Ethiopia for the management of psyllids on citrus.
